design_detail: Narrative review in the Current Opinion format of research on using several substances, said to cover work published mainly in the preceding 18 months: definitions and the DSM-5 changes, reasons for use, prevalence and latent-class patterns, psychiatric and physical health correlates, imaging and neuropsychology, and prevention and treatment. No search strategy, inclusion criteria or appraisal of the cited studies; 71 numbered references, those judged of special or outstanding interest annotated by the authors. University of Queensland group; published July 2014.
can_establish: How polysubstance use was defined and measured in research of about 2012–2014, which latent-class patterns those studies reported, and where the authors judged the evidence on harms, prevention and treatment to be thin as of 2014.
cannot_establish: Prevalence in any population beyond the cited sources (figures are second-hand and mix national surveys with student, clinical and rave samples); whether using several substances causes the mental-health, physical-health or cognitive differences described (the cited studies are mostly cross-sectional associations); or the size of any effect.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited sources include 2013 surveys from the USA, UK, Australia, Denmark and Latin America, student surveys (US and Brazilian college students), clinical and treatment samples, studies of club and rave attenders, and small imaging studies (pp. 270–272).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: None stated; the review examines key research published mainly over the previous 18 months (p. 270).
sample.selection_effects: Evidence chosen and annotated by the authors. At least 8 of 71 references name a review author among their listed authors (refs 13, 22, 23, 32, 33, 41, 66, 68; several lists end in et al.), including the Australian latent-class studies that supply several prevalence figures and correlates (refs 22 and 23, both marked of outstanding interest) and the treatment-sample latent-class study of people using cannabis (ref. 41, also marked of outstanding interest).

exposure.measurement: As in the cited studies: lifetime use, use in the past 1 to 12 months, or simultaneous use (several substances on the same occasion), mostly by self-report in surveys, grouped by latent class analysis (p. 270).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. The authors note that most population research recorded only frequency of use, not diagnostic criteria or severity (p. 270), and call for profiles that include frequency and severity (p. 273).
exposure.polysubstance: The topic of the review. Simultaneous use is described as hard to capture in surveys because of the number of possible drug pairs, and mostly studied in smaller high-risk samples (p. 270).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable; the imaging study described in most detail tested people after 1 month of abstinence (ref. 51, p. 272).

comparison.controls: As in the cited studies: latent classes using no or few substances; healthy controls or alcohol-dependent-only groups in imaging studies; patients using no other illicit substances in the treatment sample (pp. 271–272).
comparison.matching: Not described for any cited study.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not discussed. Pre-existing differences and socioeconomic disadvantage (which the review lists as a correlate of polysubstance use, p. 270) are not considered as alternative explanations for the health and cognitive associations.

outcomes.instruments: As cited: psychological distress, anxiety and depression symptoms, generalized anxiety and major depressive disorder diagnoses, psychotic symptoms, sexual risk behaviour, infectious disease, overdose, magnetic resonance spectroscopy metabolites, grey-matter volume, neuropsychological tests and prevention outcomes (pp. 271–273).
outcomes.validity_norms: Not appraised. The authors note that the reliability of clinical assessment of the DSM-5 severity index was not yet known (p. 270) and that neuroimaging studies may lack power (p. 272).
outcomes.operationalization: Wide-ranging (extended-range) polysubstance use defined by latent-class membership in each cited study; health harms defined by the cited studies' measures.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, without appraisal: rave attenders up to 75% using several substances, average five drugs at the last rave (ref. 12, p. 270); limited-range use reported by 18% of 12–17-year-olds (lifetime, ref. 23) to 34% before age 16 (ref. 18); extended-range use 2% at 12–17 vs 13.5% at 18–29 (refs 22, 23); a sedative-and-alcohol cluster with last-year prevalence 1.3% among young Australian adults (ref. 22) (p. 271). US National Survey on Drug Use and Health: non-medical prescription drug use 6.3% in the past year and 2.7% in the past month; pain relievers 4.8%, tranquillizers 2.1%, stimulants 1.2%, sedatives 0.3%; 14.4–15.5% at 18–25, 7.8–8.7% at 12–17, 3.8–4.8% at 26 and older; lifetime non-medical benzodiazepine use 7.5% in US high-school seniors (refs 34, 35; p. 271). Danish national sample: odds ratio 27 (95% CI 14.85–49.15) for long-term benzodiazepine misuse in people with long-term opioid use and chronic pain compared with individuals without chronic pain (ref. 6, p. 272).
analysis.covariates: Not applicable; adjustment in the cited studies is not described.
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. Null behavioural differences between people using several substances and controls are reported in the body (p. 272) but are absent from the abstract and the conclusion, which state cognitive deficits as established.
analysis.power: Not applicable; the authors say low statistical power may affect the neuroimaging studies (refs 61, 63; p. 272).

interpretation_gap.results_show: A descriptive account of recent studies: definitions of polysubstance use vary (lifetime, recent, same occasion); latent-class studies find limited, moderate and extended ranges of use; extended-range use is more common in young adults, in men and in club, rave, treatment-seeking and other high-risk samples; extended-range classes report more distress, anxiety, depression and sexual risk; some imaging studies find metabolite and grey-matter differences, while several find no behavioural difference from controls; prevention evidence is weak.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The conclusion opens: "It is clear that individuals who use multiple substances are at elevated risk" of comorbid psychiatric and other health conditions, and adds that they have more pervasive cognitive deficits that place them at risk of poorer treatment outcomes (p. 273); the abstract likewise lists deficits in cognitive functioning. Gaps: (1) the cited evidence is mostly cross-sectional latent-class associations, so 'risk of developing' is causal wording the designs cannot support; (2) the imaging section itself reports no behavioural difference from controls in several studies (refs 55–58) before concluding that polysubstance use is clearly associated with deficits in brain function and cognition (p. 272); (3) no study of treatment outcomes by cognitive status is described; (4) a cross-sectional contrast between age groups in two samples is read as a risk of expanding use over time, and a cross-sectional comparison after 1 month of abstinence as suggesting that cocaine may be more injurious than alcohol (pp. 271–272); (5) socioeconomic disadvantage and pre-existing differences are not weighed as explanations.

timeline.event: Fernández-Calderón et al., cluster analysis of polysubstance use in underground rave attenders (ref. 12): source of the up-to-75% figure.

Quek et al. and White et al. (review authors' group), latent class analyses of Australian national samples of young adults and adolescents (refs 22, 23): sources of the 2%, 13.5%, 18% and 1.3% figures.
Connor et al., latent class analysis of 826 people referred for cannabis treatment (ref. 41, size from the reference annotation): wide-ranging class with more psychopathology.

Liu et al., review of polysubstance use in cocaine research: alcohol and cannabis use alongside cocaine common in every sample; human imaging studies seldom excluded people who drink or use cannabis (as summarized on the project's card sc_liu_2018).

replication.where_it_stands: Citable for definitions, the variety of ways polysubstance use is measured, the latent-class pattern of limited, moderate and extended ranges, and the authors' view (2014) that research on prevention and treatment for polysubstance use was underdeveloped. Prevalence figures and health associations should be cited from the primary surveys or from the systematic reviews of latent-class studies on the project's list (Tomczyk et al., 2016, adolescents; LeComte et al., 2025, adults; not yet appraised).

The authors thank Wayne Hall for reviewing earlier versions (Acknowledgements, p. 273).
funding.declared_conflicts: There are no conflicts of interest (as printed, p. 273).
funding.affiliations_note: Centre for Youth Substance Abuse Research and Discipline of Psychiatry, The University of Queensland, and the Alcohol and Drug Assessment Unit, Princess Alexandra Hospital, Brisbane. Several cited Australian studies, and the treatment-sample latent-class study, are by the authors' group and are highlighted by them as of outstanding interest. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Standard definitions of concurrent and simultaneous polysubstance use applied in repeated national surveys; panel studies following the same people from adolescence to young adulthood (latent transition analysis) to observe changes in range of use; prospective cohorts measuring mental health and cognition before multiple-substance use begins, with adjustment for socioeconomic disadvantage and earlier difficulties; and randomized trials comparing concurrent with sequential treatment of several substance problems.

domains.note: No search, dates or criteria beyond a focus on the previous 18 months; the authors chose and annotated the evidence.

No study-by-study appraisal and designs are seldom named (two age-group samples are called panel designs); convenience samples (rave attenders) sit beside national surveys. Some limitations are named: low power in neuroimaging, weak methods in prevention research, unknown reliability of the DSM-5 severity index.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: At least 8 of 71 references are by review authors, including the Australian prevalence and correlate studies and the treatment-sample latent-class study, which the authors mark as of outstanding interest.

Causal and certain wording from cross-sectional associations (risk of developing comorbid conditions; alcohol use increases the risk of experimenting with smoking; limited-range use may increase later expansion; cocaine may be more injurious than alcohol), and a conclusion of clear cognitive deficits next to null behavioural findings.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence on harms of polysubstance use
domains.note: Studies finding no behavioural difference from controls are reported but dropped from the abstract and conclusion; explanations other than harm from the substances (socioeconomic disadvantage, pre-existing differences, selection into clinical samples) are under-represented.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the editors' checklist is used and the overall judgment can be no milder than the worst domain. The review is a useful map of definitions, measurement approaches and latent-class patterns as of 2014, but its selection is unsystematic, part of its evidence is the authors' own, and its conclusions use causal and certain language the cited designs cannot support. Citable for: definitions and measurement issues, the latent-class pattern, and the authors' 2014 view that prevention and treatment research for polysubstance use was underdeveloped. Not citable for: prevalence figures or health and cognitive harms as established facts; claims resting on it alone stay at draft and say their figures are second-hand.

key_findings.finding: Polysubstance use is defined broadly as using more than one drug over a defined period, at the same time or at different times, for therapeutic or recreational purposes; in prevention and treatment it usually means several illicit drugs but can include licit and prescription drugs used non-medically.

DSM-IV polysubstance dependence (use of three or more substances other than caffeine and nicotine with no single substance dominating, dependence criteria met for the substances as a group but not for any one) was removed in DSM-5, where substance use disorders are diagnosed by substance and graded on a severity continuum from 2 (mild) to 11 (severe) criteria; most population research records only frequency of use, not criteria or severity.

Measures of polysubstance use in 2013 surveys were based on lifetime use (refs 18, 23, 24, 26), use in the past 1 to 12 months (refs 19–22, 25–27) or simultaneous use on the same occasion (refs 22, 26); simultaneous use is hard to capture in surveys and has mostly been studied in smaller high-risk samples (club or bar patrons, clinical populations).
key_findings.locator: Prevalence and the Current Patterns of Multiple Substance Use, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Latent class analyses typically find a limited-range class (alcohol, tobacco, cannabis), a moderate-range class (adding amphetamine derivatives) and an extended-range class (adding non-medical use of prescription drugs and other illicit drugs); Figure 1 is a conceptual diagram, not to scale.
key_findings.locator: Prevalence and the Current Patterns of Multiple Substance Use, 2nd paragraph (p. 270, continuing on p. 271); Figure 1 (p. 271)

key_findings.finding: Among teenagers, limited-range use was most common, reported by 18% of 12–17-year-olds (lifetime, ref. 23) to 34% before age 16 (ref. 18). Extended-range use was 2% at 12–17 years and 13.5% at 18–29 years (refs 22, 23), which the review calls panel survey designs and reads as limited-range use in adolescence possibly increasing the risk of expanded use in young adulthood.
key_findings.locator: Prevalence section, 3rd paragraph and 5th paragraph (right column) (p. 271); annotations to references 22 and 23 (p. 274)
key_findings.note: The reference annotations describe refs 22 and 23 as nationally representative samples of young adults and of adolescents respectively and say nothing of following the same people over time; the annotation of ref. 22 gives 13.2% for polydrug use, against 13.5% in the text.

key_findings.finding: US National Survey on Drug Use and Health (ref. 34): non-medical prescription drug use 6.3% in the past year and 2.7% in the past month in people aged over 12 (as printed); pain relievers 4.8%, tranquillizers 2.1%, stimulants 1.2%, sedatives 0.3%; higher at 18–25 years (14.4–15.5%) than at 12–17 (7.8–8.7%) or 26 and older (3.8–4.8%). Lifetime non-medical benzodiazepine use was 7.5% in a national sample of US high-school seniors (ref. 35).

Women and men: some evidence that polysubstance use involving non-medical prescription drugs is higher in young adult women than men (refs 19, 26); young adult men (about 18–35 years) are at higher risk of extended-range use (refs 22, 26, 27, 39); other correlates are being single, having low education and being employed (refs 21, 22). A small cluster of sedative and alcohol use had last-year prevalence of 1.3% among young Australian adults (ref. 22).
key_findings.locator: Prevalence section, 4th and 5th paragraphs (right column) (p. 271); annotations to references 19 and 26 (p. 274)
key_findings.note: Both sources for the sex difference are student samples by their annotations (US first-year college students, ref. 19; Brazilian college students, n = 12,544, ref. 26), measured by self-report; adjustment is not described. The annotation of ref. 26 says 18–34-year-old men were the most likely to report polydrug use.

key_findings.finding: Settings: up to 75% of rave attenders used several substances, with an average of five drugs at the last rave attended (ref. 12, a cluster analysis of underground rave attenders); polysubstance use in club and dance venues is described as widespread and far higher than in other venue types (refs 25, 28).
key_findings.locator: Reasons for Use, 2nd paragraph (p. 270, right column); Prevalence section, 5th paragraph (p. 271)

key_findings.finding: Health correlates from latent class analyses: classes with wide-ranging use report more psychological distress (refs 22, 23) and more anxiety and depression symptoms (ref. 31); people who drink and also use illicit drugs are more likely to have generalized anxiety and major depressive disorder (ref. 40); in a treatment-seeking cannabis sample the wide-ranging class had more depression, anxiety, manic excitement and positive psychotic symptoms than patients using no other illicit drugs (ref. 41); latent class studies also link polysubstance use with sexual risk behaviour and infectious disease (refs 42, 43).

Benzodiazepines with opioids: in a Danish national sample (ref. 6), people with long-term opioid use and chronic pain had an odds ratio of 27 (95% CI 14.85–49.15) for long-term benzodiazepine misuse compared with individuals without chronic pain; people using both drug classes are described as at higher risk of non-fatal and fatal overdose (ref. 48), comorbid conditions and forensic problems (ref. 7).
key_findings.locator: Comorbid Psychopathology and Health, 2nd paragraph (p. 271, continuing on p. 272)
key_findings.note: The comparison group is described only as individuals without chronic pain; whether they also used opioids cannot be told from the review.

key_findings.finding: Imaging: after 1 month of abstinence, people dependent on alcohol and on one or more stimulants (mostly cocaine) had lower N-acetylaspartate, creatine, myo-inositol and choline-containing metabolites in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex than people dependent on alcohol alone, who did not differ from controls; N-acetylaspartate correlated with visuospatial and working-memory performance (ref. 51). Abstinent people using several substances had less grey matter in the right temporal pole and medial frontal lobe (ref. 50). In neither metabolite study were the abnormalities related to severity of use.

Several of these imaging studies, and recent studies of inhibitory control (ref. 57) and decision-making (ref. 58), found no difference in behavioural performance between people using several substances and controls; large differences were reported on standard tests given outside the scanner in another study (ref. 62), in which only severity of cocaine use was related to brain metabolism.
key_findings.locator: Imaging and Neuropsychology Studies, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Prevention and treatment: school and community programmes to reduce youth substance use show modest efficacy, with small short-term effects and poor longer-term outcomes (refs 64–66); pervasive methodological weaknesses prevent conclusions about prevention aimed at adults who use several substances (ref. 67); there is limited evidence on whether treating several substance problems at once works better than treating them one after another; personality-targeted prevention has reported promising results at 24 months (ref. 71).
key_findings.locator: Prevention, Treatment, and Further Research, 1st paragraph (p. 272, continuing on p. 273) and 2nd paragraph (p. 273)

key_findings.finding: Energy drinks with alcohol: experimental studies at low doses of caffeine and alcohol did not find increased short-term behavioural effects or a higher perceived level of intoxication (refs 15, 16); a commentary (ref. 17) argues that laboratory doses are lower than those drunk in real settings and calls for research independent of industry funding.
key_findings.locator: Reasons for Use, 3rd paragraph (p. 270); annotations to references 15–17 (p. 274)
key_findings.note: The annotations to refs 15 and 16 state that their authors acknowledged a conflict of interest with an energy-drink company; ref. 15 is described as a double-blind four-arm crossover trial in 52 volunteers.

key_findings.finding: The authors conclude that people who use several substances are at elevated risk of comorbid psychiatric and other health conditions and have more pervasive cognitive deficits that place them at risk of poorer treatment outcomes, and that prevention and treatment approaches for polysubstance use are underdeveloped compared with those for single substances.

reporting_issues.issue: The contrast of extended-range use at 12–17 years (2%) and 18–29 years (13.5%) is attributed to panel survey designs, but the two cited sources (refs 22, 23) are annotated as nationally representative samples of different age groups, with no follow-up of the same people described.
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures compare age groups in two samples; they do not show that adolescents' limited-range use expands later, which the paragraph infers.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives 13.5% for extended-range use at 18–29 years (refs 22, 23), while the annotation to ref. 22 gives a polydrug-use prevalence of 13.2% in young Australian adults.
reporting_issues.consequence: The two figures may describe different quantities; the primary paper is needed before either is cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Ref. 26 is cited for higher polysubstance use involving non-medical prescription drugs in young women than men, but its annotation reports that 18–34-year-old men were the most likely to report polydrug use.
reporting_issues.consequence: Not necessarily contradictory (different outcomes), but the support for a sex difference rests on two student samples and cannot be checked from the review.

reporting_issues.issue: The Danish odds ratio (27, 95% CI 14.85–49.15) compares people with long-term opioid use and chronic pain against individuals without chronic pain, without saying whether the comparison group used opioids; the outcome is called long-term use of benzodiazepines abuse.
reporting_issues.consequence: The contrast actually estimated cannot be identified from the review; ref. 6 must be read before the figure is used.

reporting_issues.issue: The US survey prevalence is given for people aged over 12, and the age-group figures are ranges (for example 14.4–15.5% at 18–25) without saying what the ranges span (years, drug types or estimates).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figures cannot be quoted precisely without the source report (ref. 34).
